reason: The provided sources fully support a compelling and surprising short with over 10 distinct, two-source verified claims.
story: For generations, we have been told that the Great Wall of China is the only human-made object visible from the Moon with the naked eye. But that is a total myth. According to NASA and optics experts, you cannot see it from the Moon at all, and astronauts struggle to spot it even from low Earth orbit. The wall is roughly ten times too narrow for the human eye to resolve from 400 kilometers up. Plus, because builders used local stone and rammed earth, the structure blends right into the surrounding terrain through a natural camouflage effect. Even China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, admitted he could not see it from space. So while the Great Wall is an incredible architectural feat stretching over 13,000 miles, it remains completely invisible to astronauts without the help of a telephoto lens.
angle: The most famous 'fact' about the Great Wall of China—that you can see it from the Moon—is a complete myth, and astronauts can barely spot it from low Earth orbit.

claims.claim: The Great Wall cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
Astronauts struggle to spot the Great Wall even from low Earth orbit.
The wall is roughly ten times too narrow for the human eye to resolve from the International Space Station.
The building materials cause a camouflage effect, making the wall blend into the surrounding terrain.
China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, stated he could not see the Great Wall from space.
The myth of the wall's lunar visibility can be traced back to a 1754 letter by English antiquary William Stukeley.
Richard Halliburton's 1938 book further popularized the Moon visibility myth.
A comprehensive survey released in 2012 by China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage put the total length at 21,196.18 km (13,170.70 mi).
No human bones were ever incorporated into the mortar or any part of the wall.
Astronaut Leroy Chiao managed to photograph sections of the wall from the ISS using a telephoto lens.
The wall can be seen readily in radar imagery taken from space.
Emperor Qin Shi Huang initiated the connection of wall sections around 220 BC.

disputed: Whether human bodies were buried inside the wall is treated as a legend/falsehood by some sources (S1, S6) while another source refers to worker deaths earning it the moniker 'longest cemetery on Earth' (S5); scripts should attribute bones to urban legend.
